Two students who love cars

We are Maruan and Cesar, two Queen's students who love cars. We started Drive Smart because not everyone has a "car friend". In surveys, 70% of first-time buyers didn't really know what they were looking for, and 65% of Gen Z think they paid for a repair they didn't need. We want to fix that, in simple words.

Drive Smart is run by Maruan Hdioud and Cesar Breitner. Cesar writes the buying guides and films our videos. Maruan builds the site and writes the Fix Smart articles. Every post is reviewed by both of us before it goes live.

How we keep advice reliable: anyone can read, members post with a free account, enthusiasts get a Verified badge after a short car-knowledge check, and we review what gets published.

Our top 2 first cars under $10k

CBBy Cesar Breitner · Editor · 4 min read

If you have around $10,000 and you just want a car that starts every morning, these are the two we would buy first. Both are everywhere in Kingston, parts are cheap, and any mechanic knows them.

1. Toyota Corolla (2013–2016)

The Corolla is the car your parents would pick for you, and they would be right. It is not exciting, but it is very reliable and cheap to keep on the road. Insurance is usually reasonable too.

What to check

  • Service records, especially regular oil changes.
  • Rust under the doors and around the rear wheels (road salt is the enemy in Ontario).
  • On a test drive, the automatic should feel smooth, with no jerks.

Fair price: $8,000 to $11,000, depending on kilometres and condition.

2. Honda Civic (2012–2015)

The Civic is a bit more fun to drive than the Corolla and very good on gas. It is one of the most common used cars in Canada, so you will have plenty of choice.

What to check

  • Turn the AC on full. If it blows warm, the repair can be expensive, so negotiate the price down.
  • Look for rust behind the rear wheels.
  • Ask if it was modified. A lowered or loud Civic was probably driven hard.

Fair price: $7,000 to $10,500.

Before you hand over the money

Whatever you choose, book a pre-purchase inspection at an independent mechanic. It costs a little, but it can save you thousands. And if a seller asks way more than the fair range, walk away. There are always other Corollas.

I hear a squeal when I brake. Do I need new pads?

MHBy Maruan Hdioud · Editor · 4 min read

You press the brake and hear a high-pitched squeal. It is the most common noise a car can make, and probably the one that scares people the most. The good news: most of the time it is not dangerous at all. It is your car politely telling you something.

Why brakes squeal

Most brake pads have a small metal tab built in. When the pad gets thin, that tab touches the disc and squeals on purpose. It is an alarm, not a breakdown. Your brakes still work, but the pads are near the end.

Other harmless reasons

  • Morning or after rain: a thin layer of rust forms on the discs overnight. The squeal goes away after a few stops.
  • Brand new pads: they can squeal for the first days while they settle.
  • Dust: brake dust between the pad and the disc, often after gravel roads.

When it becomes serious

Stop waiting and see a mechanic soon if you notice any of these:

  • A grinding metal sound instead of a squeal. The pad is gone and metal is touching metal.
  • The car pulls to one side when you brake.
  • The pedal feels soft, goes lower than usual, or vibrates.
  • A brake warning light on the dashboard.

How long can I wait?

With a squeal only, think a few weeks of normal driving, not months. If you wait until it grinds, you will need new discs too, and the bill roughly doubles.

What it should cost in Kingston

Pads only, one axle, at a garageabout $120–250
Pads and discs, one axle, at a garageabout $250–450
Pads alone, if you or a friend can do itabout $50–100

Usually only the front pads need changing, because the front brakes do most of the work. Ask the shop to show you the old pads and tell you how many millimetres are left. Most of the price is labour, so an independent garage is often cheaper than a dealer. If someone quotes "brakes all around" for $500 or more on a small car, get a second opinion.
